opus-5.5.text:
That's a distinction I think about a lot, because it shapes almost every strategic decision we make in robot learning.

Real robot data is the gold standard in one sense: it's collected on the actual embodiment, with the real sensors, the real actuators, the real physics, so there's no gap between what you train on and what you deploy on. But it's extremely expensive. You need physical robots, you need people to teleoperate them or supervise them, things break, you need to reset scenes. Even with a large fleet, you're talking about thousands or maybe tens of thousands of hours. Compare that to the internet-scale data that trained language models, and real robot data is many orders of magnitude smaller. It grows roughly linearly with the money and human effort you put in, so it doesn't scale the way we'd like.

Scalable data sources are the ones where the cost of adding more doesn't grow in proportion to the amount. I usually think of three big categories.

The first is simulation. Once you've built a good simulator and good environments, you can run thousands of instances in parallel on a cluster, and the marginal cost of another million episodes is basically compute. This has been very successful for locomotion. A lot of the agile legged-robot results came from training entirely in simulation and transferring zero-shot to hardware. Manipulation is harder because contact-rich interaction and deformable objects are harder to simulate faithfully, and building diverse, realistic scenes still takes a lot of human effort. That's where generative models may help a lot.

The second is internet data: text, images, and especially video of humans doing things. It has no action labels and no robot embodiment, but it contains an enormous amount of knowledge about the world: what objects are, how they're used, what tasks look like, some intuitive physics. That's why vision-language models became the backbone of robot foundation models. You get semantic understanding and generalization almost for free, and the robot data only needs to teach the last mile, grounding that knowledge into actions.

The third, more emerging category is human data collected in ways that don't require a robot, like egocentric video from wearables or handheld gripper devices that record demonstrations in the wild. You remove the robot from the collection loop, so it's much cheaper and you can go into real homes and offices for diversity.

So I don't see it as either/or. The recipe that seems to work is a pyramid: a huge base of internet and human data for broad world knowledge, a large middle layer of simulation and cross-embodiment data, and a relatively small but very high-quality top layer of real robot data on the target platform. The research question is how to make that top layer as small as possible, how much of the robot's competence you can get from the scalable sources and how efficiently you can close the remaining gap with real data. I think that ratio will determine how fast robotics can follow the scaling path that language models took.

r001.rationale: It says simulation can run thousands of instances in parallel on a cluster, with the marginal cost of more episodes being compute.

r002.rationale: It explains that real robot data requires physical robots, human teleoperation or supervision, and scene resets, making collection expensive and growth dependent on money and human effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it, real robot data is the gold standard. It's the only data that actually captures the full loop: the robot's sensors, its actuators, its own body, how the world pushes back when you touch it. Nothing else has that fidelity. But the problem is it's expensive and slow. You need a physical robot, a teleoperator, a setup, someone to reset the scene after every episode. If a human does ten demonstrations an hour, that's your throughput. You cannot scale that to the billions of examples that made language models work.

So when I say "scalable data sources," I mean anything where the cost of getting one more example goes almost to zero. Simulation is the clearest case. Once you build the environment, you can spin up thousands of copies on GPUs and generate years of experience overnight. Human video is another one. There are millions of hours of people cooking, cleaning, assembling things on the internet, and every one of those shows you something about how tasks get done, even though there's no robot in the frame. And then there's synthetic data more broadly, things like generative models producing new scenes, new object layouts, new trajectories.

The catch is that each of these has a gap with reality. Simulation has the sim-to-real gap: contact physics, deformable objects, lighting, all the stuff that's hard to model. Human video has an embodiment gap: a human hand is not a parallel gripper, and you don't see joint torques or action labels. So you get scale, but you lose grounding.

The way I distinguish them, honestly, is by asking two questions. First, what does the marginal sample cost? Real robot data costs minutes of a person's time. Scalable sources cost compute. Second, what does the data actually teach you? I've come to see scalable data as the thing that gives the model its priors: what objects look like, how tasks decompose, what plausible motions are. Real robot data is what calibrates those priors to a specific body in the physical world. You need a lot of the first and a smaller but very targeted amount of the second.

So I don't think of them as competing. The right recipe is something like a pyramid. A huge base of internet-scale and simulated data, a middle layer of cross-embodiment robot data from many labs and platforms, and then a small, high-quality top layer of data from the actual robot you're deploying. The real data is irreplaceable, but it should be the last mile, not the whole road.

r001.rationale: The response says scalable sources cost compute and describes running thousands of simulation copies on GPUs to generate years of experience overnight, communicating computation as the means of scaling data supply.

r002.rationale: It attributes real robot data’s cost and slow throughput to needing a physical robot, a teleoperator, a setup, and scene resets after episodes.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by how the data is collected and what it tells us about the physical world. Real robot data comes from a robot interacting with its environment. You have observations, actions, and the consequences of those actions. That’s very valuable because it directly captures the problem we want the robot to solve, but collecting it requires hardware, time, maintenance, and often human supervision.

Scalable data sources include things like simulation and human videos. In simulation, you can run many robots in parallel and generate experience much faster. With video, you can learn from human activity without operating a robot for every example. But there’s a gap: simulation may not capture the physics perfectly, and videos generally don’t tell you the forces or robot actions needed to reproduce what you see.

So these sources are complementary. Scalable data can give you broad knowledge and useful behaviors, while real robot data helps ground that knowledge in what actually happens when the robot acts.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation can generate experience faster and videos avoid operating a robot for every example, but it does not identify computation as the means of supplying effectively unlimited data.

r002.rationale: It explains that real robot data comes from robots interacting with environments and that collecting it requires hardware, time, maintenance, and often supervision.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish them by how easily we can collect more data and how directly that data matches what the robot needs to do. Scalable sources include simulation and human videos. You can generate many trials in simulation, and videos contain a huge variety of objects, environments, and behaviors.

Real robot data is more expensive because you need physical robots interacting with the world. You have hardware maintenance, safety constraints, and resets between attempts. But that data captures the robot’s actual observations, actions, and the consequences of those actions—especially contact and physical dynamics that are difficult to infer from video or model accurately in simulation.

So I see these sources as complementary. Scalable data can give you broad knowledge and useful representations, while real robot experience helps ground that knowledge in what the robot can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response mentions simulation and videos as sources of many trials or varied data, but does not identify computation as the means of supplying effectively unlimited data.

r002.rationale: It says real robot data is more expensive because collection requires physical robots interacting with the world, along with maintenance, safety constraints, and resets.
